passage:
Diary, Saturday
I got my hair cut short like the captain of our women's team. Everyone at the nets says I look like a boy. I don't care. I'm the only girl there anyway. I practised her stance for one hour in the garage: bat up high, chin down, eyes still. I even did her little double tap of the bat before each ball. At the nets I hit three fours in a row!! I felt STRONG.
But then I copied the other thing she does, pointing the bat at the bowler after a four. Minakshi was bowling and she stopped smiling. Coach said, "Hit hard. No pointing." I felt silly.
Tomorrow: same stance, no pointing. The captain always shakes hands after matches too. I'll copy that.
Sharmila

qa.q: How many fours did Sharmila hit in a row at the nets?
qa.a: Three fours in a row.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila feel 'STRONG' when she used the captain's stance?
qa.a: Copying her hero made her feel some of the captain's power and confidence, and hitting fours seemed to prove it. 😊

qa.q: What choice did Sharmila make about which habits to copy, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping the stance and the handshakes but dropping the pointing, because the handshake shows respect while the pointing only upset Minakshi.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Sharmila pointed the bat at her?
qa.a: Minakshi probably felt mocked or shown up, which is why she stopped smiling.

grounding: A girl copies her cricket hero's haircut, stance and gestures, feels stronger, and learns the swagger doesn't come with the skill.

passage:
Nine-year-old Indu, in her village outside Karnal, had pinned up a newspaper photo of the district's gold-medal sprinter, a young woman who had grown up three villages away. Indu now tied her hair in the same high knot, wore a sweatband on one wrist, and started every morning with the warm-up she had seen on the TV at the tea stall. She even walked like her, shoulders back. "Early to bed, early to track," she told her little sister Payal, in the sprinter's firm voice.
But when Payal beat her in a race to the well, Indu snapped, "Champions don't lose to babies," and stalked off. Payal's lip wobbled. That evening Indu came back with a guava. "Champions also say sorry," she mumbled.

qa.q: What did Indu wear on one wrist?
qa.a: A sweatband.

qa.q: Why did Indu snap 'Champions don't lose to babies' at Payal?
qa.a: Losing hurt her new champion image, and she borrowed a proud, swaggering attitude to cover the embarrassment.

qa.q: What turning point shows Indu choosing the better part of her hero?
qa.a: Coming back with a guava and saying 'Champions also say sorry', which keeps the discipline and drops the swagger.

qa.q: How might Payal feel about her sister's new champion act?
qa.a: Admiring at first, then hurt when the swagger turned on her; the apology probably made her feel close again.

grounding: A village girl copies a local sprinting champion's style and voice, feels stronger, and briefly borrows the swagger too.

passage:
At his Saturday cricket club in south London, eleven-year-old Jin had started copying his favourite batter from the television: the same blond streak in his fringe (his mum had allowed one), the same wide stance, the same slow walk to the crease. With the stance, his drives actually got better. He felt taller walking out. Chidi, who opened the batting with him, said, "You look like a proper pro."
But Jin also started copying the batter's hard stare at bowlers and the muttering at umpires. When the club umpire gave him out leg before wicket, Jin threw his bat down. Coach took him aside. "Your hero hits beautifully. Copy that. And copy how he apologises afterwards, too." Jin went red and picked up his bat.

qa.q: What did Jin's mum allow him to dye?
qa.a: One blond streak in his fringe.

qa.q: Why did Jin feel taller walking out to bat?
qa.a: Copying his hero's stance and walk made him feel some of the batter's strength and confidence, and his better drives seemed to prove it.

qa.q: What choice did Coach help Jin see?
qa.a: To keep copying the good batting and the apologies, but drop the stare and the bat-throwing swagger.

qa.q: How might the club umpire have felt when Jin threw his bat?
qa.a: Disrespected and uncomfortable, since a young player was treating a fair decision as an insult.

grounding: A boy in London copies a cricket hero's look and stance, feels stronger, and also picks up the hero's swagger.

passage:
At the district cricket academy, Shalini, eleven, had become someone else. Her favourite fast bowler wore a tight side braid, so Shalini did too. She copied the long run-up, the hard stare down the pitch, the knee-slide after a wicket. She arrived at six to do the bowler's shadow drills from a video, and her line had never been better.
On Thursday she bowled a small Class 3 boy, then walked up to him and said, "Go home, baby," just like the clip. A few kids laughed. The boy's lip shook.
Coach Lalremsiami called Shalini over. "Your run-up is superb. Coming at six is exactly what your hero does. The 'go home, baby' part, though? Would she say that to a little kid?"
Shalini looked at her shoes. "Maybe not to a little kid."

qa.q: What did Shalini say to the Class 3 boy she bowled?
qa.a: "Go home, baby."

qa.q: Why might copying the fast bowler's stare and celebration feel good to Shalini?
qa.a: Copying her hero makes Shalini feel powerful and confident, and that confidence pushes her to train harder too.

qa.q: What choice by Coach Lalremsiami sorted the good from the bad?
qa.a: The coach praised the run-up and the early training but questioned the sledge, helping Shalini keep the hero's values and drop the swagger.

qa.q: What was that moment like for the Class 3 boy?
qa.a: Already out, he was mocked by an older player in front of others, so he likely felt small and embarrassed, fighting tears.

grounding: Shows a child who copies a fast bowler's style and training, gaining strength and discipline but also picking up swagger that a coach helps separate.

passage:
I'm Harsha, and I run the Sunday cricket in our colony lane. For a month Gargi, nine, has been turning into her favourite batter. Same short haircut, same tap-tap of the bat on the ground, same slow twirl after every shot. She even practises forward defence a hundred times against our wall before school, because she read that her hero does.
Her batting really has got better. But last Sunday, when Sunny gave her out lbw, she threw her head back, rolled her eyes like on TV, and walked off without the handshake. Nobody knew what to say.
I don't know what she was thinking. Maybe she felt like a star. Later I saw her sitting on the steps, bat across her knees, watching the others play.

qa.q: How many times does Gargi practise forward defence before school?
qa.a: A hundred times, against the wall.

qa.q: What might Gargi have felt as she rolled her eyes and walked off?
qa.a: She may have felt like a real star copying her hero, but the swagger also covered disappointment at getting out; sitting alone later suggests it didn't feel good.

qa.q: How could Harsha help Gargi keep the good parts of copying her hero?
qa.a: Harsha could praise the practice and the improved batting, then remind Gargi that the handshake is part of the game, even for stars.

qa.q: How might Sunny have felt when Gargi rolled her eyes at the lbw decision?
qa.a: Sunny was only doing the umpire's job, so the eye-roll probably felt unfair and awkward, and might make Sunny unsure about umpiring again.

grounding: Illustrates, through an older neighbour's eyes, a child who adopts a batter's look and practice habits, improving her game but also importing an eye-rolling swagger.
